text: The Taj Mahal, meaning "Crown of the Palace" in Urdu and derived from Arabic and Persian words for "crown" and "palace," is an ivory-white marble mausoleum located on the right bank of the Yamuna river in Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India. It was commissioned in 1631 by Shah Jahan (r. 1628–1658), the fifth Mughal emperor, to house the tomb of his beloved wife, Mumtaz Mahal, who died on 17 June 1631 while giving birth to their 14th child, Gauhara Begum. Construction began in 1632, with the mausoleum completed in 1648 and the surrounding buildings and garden finished in 1653. The first ceremony held at the site was on 6 February 1643, marking the 12th anniversary of Mumtaz Mahal's death. The entire complex, spanning 17 hectares (42 acres), includes a mosque, a guest house, and formal gardens bounded on three sides by a crenellated wall. The building complex incorporates Indo-Islamic and Mughal architectural traditions, featuring symmetrical designs with various shapes and symbols. The mausoleum is constructed of white marble inlaid with semi-precious stones, while red sandstone is used for other structures, similar to Mughal-era buildings. The complex sits on a 300-metre (980 ft) long by 8.7-metre (28.5 ft) high platform built with varying patterns of dark and light sandstone. The mausoleum itself stands on a 6-metre (20 ft) high square plinth measuring 95.5 metres (313 ft) per side, with a large multi-chambered cube and chamfered corners forming an eight-sided structure approximately 57.3 metres (188 ft) long. It has four identical sides with iwans (arch-shaped doorways), each topped by a 33-metre (108 ft) high pishtaq (vaulted archway) and two arched balconies, replicated on chamfered corners for symmetry. Access to the mausoleum is provided by two flights of stairs on the southern side. The central feature is a 23-metre (75 ft) high marble dome on a 12-metre (39 ft) high cylindrical drum with an inner diameter of 18.4 metres (60 ft), slightly asymmetrical and topped by a 9.6-metre (31 ft) high gilded finial. Four smaller chattris, shaped like the main dome, are placed at the corners, supported by columns and decorated with lotus motifs. Tall guldastas extend from the walls as decorative spires. The main dome and chattris are adorned with Persian and Indian design elements, with the main finial originally made of gold and later replaced by a gilded bronze copy in the early 19th century, topped by a moon motif pointing heavenward. Four minarets, each over 40 metres (130 ft) tall, flank the tomb at the corners of the plinth, each composed of three equal parts with balconies and smaller chattris, designed to fall away from the tomb in case of collapse. The external surfaces are decorated with delicate reliefs, inlays, and carvings using precious and semi-precious stones, including pietra dura inlays of geometric patterns of vines, flowers, and fruits. The calligraphy on the gateway arches, composed of thuluth script in jasper or black marble inlaid in white marble, includes Qur'anic passages, with one on the southern gate translating to "O Soul, thou art at rest. Return to the Lord at peace with Him, and He at peace with you." This calligraphy is attributed to Abdul Haq, who was granted the title "Amanat Khan" by Shah Jahan. The main chamber is an octagon with 7.3-metre (24 ft) sides, with two tiers of eight pishtaq arches along the walls, and balconies on the central upper arches, each with intricate jali windows. The inner walls are open along the axes with jali screens transmitting light from outside. The chamber has an open elongated room on three sides, flanked by square cells with decorated ceilings, likely used for visitors and Qur'an reciters. Staircases lead to the roof level, with ventilation shafts. The interior walls are 25 metres (82 ft) high and topped by a "false" interior dome with a sun motif, decorated with inlay work of gemstones. The walls are highly decorated with dado bas-reliefs, intricate lapidary inlays, and calligraphy. The main chamber contains the false cenotaphs of Mumtaz Mahal and Shah Jahan, with the real tombs located in the basement. The cenotaphs are aligned north–south, with heads facing north and bodies laid on their sides with faces turned toward the west, facing Mecca. Mumtaz's cenotaph is centered on a 1.5 by 2.5-metre (4 ft 11 in by 8 ft 2 in) marble base, and Shah Jahan's is on a larger base to the west, marked by a small pen box sculpture. The cenotaphs are adorned with detailed inlays: Mumtaz's features natural plum fruits, buds, and blossoms with the epitaph "The illumined grave of Arjumand Bano Begam, entided Mumtaz Mahal, who died in the year 1631," and Shah Jahan's has a similar decoration with the epitaph "This is the sacred grave of His Most Exalted Majesty... Shah Jahan, Padshah; may it ever be fragrant! The year 1076 [AD 1666]." The original burial chamber is undecorated, with the Ninety Nine Names of God inscribed on its side. The complex is set within a charbagh garden, inspired by Persian gardens and symbolizing Paradise (Jannah), divided into four quadrants by walkways and further subdivided into 16 sunken parterres. A raised marble water tank, called al Hawd al-Kawthar, is positioned halfway between the tomb and the gateway on a north–south axis, reflecting the mausoleum. The garden includes avenues of trees and fountains, and in the north-western quadrant, there is a site marking where Mumtaz Mahal was first buried before being moved to the main chamber. The tomb is located at the end of the garden, unlike most Mughal gardens, and the Archaeological Survey of India has hypothesized that the Yamuna river was incorporated into the design as one of the rivers of Paradise, based on the discovery of Mahtab Bagh on the opposite bank. The Taj Mahal was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983 for being "the jewel of Islamic art in India and one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage." It is regarded as one of the best examples of Mughal architecture and a symbol of Indian history. It is a major tourist attraction, drawing over five million visitors annually, and was declared a winner of the New 7 Wonders of the World in 2007. The Taj Mahal and its surroundings are a Monument of National Importance, administered by the Archaeological Survey of India. The construction project employed more than 20,000 workers and artisans under the guidance of a board of architects led by Ustad Ahmad Lahori, the emperor's court architect. The complex was completed at a cost estimated at the time to be around ₹32 million, equivalent to approximately ₹52.8 billion (US$827 million) in 2015. Abdul Hamid Lahori, in his 1636 book Padshahnama, refers to the Taj Mahal as rauza-i munawwara, meaning the illumined or illustrious tomb. The imperial court records illustrate Shah Jahan's deep grief, including avoiding royal affairs for a week and giving up music and lavish dressing for two years, highlighting his devotion to Mumtaz Mahal. Shah Jahan chose the site south of Agra, where a mansion of Raja Jai Singh I stood, and in exchange, Jai Singh agreed to give the land to the emperor for a large palace in the center of Agra. The design of the Taj Mahal draws inspiration from Timurid and Mughal buildings, including the Gur-e Amir in Samarkand and Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, which influenced the Charbagh gardens and hasht-behesht plan. The entire complex is symmetrical, with the use of various shapes and symbols, and the use of contrasting colors and tessellation patterns in floors and walkways. The plinth is differentiated by an interlocking pattern of octagonal white marble pieces set into four-pointed stars made of red sandstone, surrounded by a border. The building features many lattice windows or jalis with interlocking hexagonal patterns. The calligraphy on the buildings was created in 1609 by Abdul Haq, and the inscription at the base of the interior dome reads "Written by the insignificant being, Amanat Khan Shirazi."

The Taj Mahal complex, built between 1631 and 1653, was commissioned by Shah Jahan in exchange for a palace in Agra from Raja Jai Singh I, and construction began in 1632. The site, located south of the walled city of Agra, was prepared by excavating an area of about 1.2 hectares (3 acres), filling it with dirt to reduce seepage, and leveling it at 50 metres (160 ft) above the riverbank. The tomb complex was constructed primarily of brick and lime mortar, with the external surface and interior of the main cenotaph veneered in white marble from Makrana, Rajasthan, and other interior surfaces and accessory buildings lined with red sandstone from Fatehpur Sikri, Uttar Pradesh, coated with a red octet. Over 28 types of precious and semi-precious stones, including jade, crystal from China, turquoise from Tibet, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, sapphire from Sri Lanka, and carnelian from Arabia, were inlaid into the white marble. More than 20,000 artisans, labourers, painters, and specialists—such as sculptors from Bukhara, calligraphers from Syria and Persia, designers from southern India, stone cutters from Baluchistan, and Italian artisans—were involved in the construction. A 15 km (9.3 mi) long earthen ramp was built to transport materials, hauled by oxen and elephants on specially constructed wagons, and a colossal brick scaffold mirrored the tomb’s structure. An elaborate post-and-beam pulley system, powered by animals, was used to raise marble blocks. Water for the gardens was drawn from the Yamuna River via animal-powered devices, transported through a channel into an underground reservoir along the eastern wall, lifted by pulleys and wheels to a tank, and then carried via an aqueduct southward to the western wall before turning east. The water was distributed through earthenware pipes underground, with fountains in the central tank powered by the drop from 9.47 m (31.1 ft) high walls, using large copper vessels interconnected by copper pipes. The charbagh garden, inspired by Persian gardens, symbolizes the Paradise garden (Jannah) with four rivers flowing from a central spring or mountain, dividing the garden into four quadrants. The main tomb is located at the end of the garden, unlike most Mughal gardens which place a tomb in the center. The north-western quadrant marks the site where Mumtaz Mahal was first buried before being moved to the main chamber. The discovery of Mahtab Bagh on the other side of the Yamuna river led the Archaeological Survey of India to hypothesize that the river itself was incorporated into the garden design as one of the rivers of Paradise. Similarities in layout and architectural features with the Shalimar Gardens suggest both may have been designed by the same architect, Ali Mardan. Early accounts describe abundant vegetation, including roses, daffodils, and fruit trees. As the Mughal Empire declined, the gardens were neglected, and when the British Raj took over, they were redesigned to resemble 19th-century London lawns. The Taj Mahal complex is enclosed by crenellated red sandstone walls on three sides, with the Yamuna-facing side open. Outside the walls are mausoleums for Shah Jahan’s other wives, royals, and favorite servants. The inner walls feature columned arcades with domed chattris and smaller structures like the Music House. The main gateway, built of marble, mirrors the tomb’s architecture and includes intricate bas-relief and pietra dura inlays. At the far end stand two similar red sandstone buildings: one a mosque and the other a jawab, lacking a mihrab. The complex was partially completed in 1643 with a ceremony held by Shah Jahan on 6 February to mark the 12th anniversary of Mumtaz Mahal’s death. Construction of the mausoleum ended in 1648, with additional work continuing for five years, and the entire complex completed in 1653 at a cost of approximately ₹32 million (equivalent to ₹52.8 billion or US$827 million in 2015). In December 1652, Aurangzeb wrote to Shah Jahan about leaks in the tomb, mosque, and assembly hall. In 1658, Shah Jahan was deposed and placed under house arrest at Agra Fort, from where he could see the Taj Mahal. Upon his death in 1666, Aurangzeb buried him next to Mumtaz Mahal. In the 18th century, the Jat rulers of Bharatpur attacked the Taj Mahal, removing two chandeliers—one agate, one silver—and the gold and silver screen; the gold shield covering the 4.6-metre-high (15 ft) finial of the main dome was also taken. By the late 19th century, the buildings fell into disrepair, and in 1908, Lord Curzon ordered and completed a restoration project, also commissioning a large interior lamp and replacing the gardens with European-style lawns. In 1942, scaffolding was erected to hide the monument from Japanese air attacks; during the 1965 and 1971 India-Pakistan wars, scaffolding was again used to mislead bomber pilots. Since Indian independence in 1947, the Archaeological Survey of India has maintained the monument. In 1983, the Taj Mahal was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site for being "the jewel of Islamic art in India and one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage." Since the late 20th century, environmental pollution, including acid rain and emissions from the Mathura Oil Refinery affecting the Yamuna River, has caused the monument to turn yellow-brown. After the Supreme Court’s 1997 ruling in M. C. Mehta v. Union of India & Ors., the Indian government established the Taj Trapezium Zone (TTZ), a 10,400-square-kilometre (4,000 sq mi) area with strict emissions standards. Concerns about structural integrity have arisen due to declining groundwater levels, with cracks appearing in 2010 and minarets showing tilting; minor damage occurred in April 2018 and May 2020. In the 2020s, the government has undertaken restoration efforts, including placing mud packs to restore the white color and replacing broken marble. The Taj Mahal is a major tourist attraction, drawing about five million visitors in the 2022–23 financial year, with a three-tier pricing system: ₹50 for Indian citizens, ₹540 for SAARC and BIMSTEC nationals, and ₹1,100 for foreign tourists. Visitors enter through three gates, and polluting vehicles are banned; tourists must walk or take electric buses from designated parking areas. The complex is open daily except Fridays, from one hour before sunrise to 45 minutes before sunset, and limited night viewing is offered on full moon days, excluding Ramadan. In 2019, fines were introduced for visitors staying over three hours. A 2025 government report stated the Taj Mahal earned ₹297 crore (US$35 million) over five years, making it the highest-earning ASI monument. The small town of Taj Ganji or Mumtazabad, located south of the Taj, was built with caravanserais, bazaars, and markets to serve visitors and workers. The Taj Mahal is frequently listed in travel guides and the New Seven Wonders of the World (a 2007 poll), and is a common destination for foreign dignitaries. The monument has long been admired across cultures, with personal and emotional responses surpassing scholarly analysis. A myth claims Shah Jahan planned a black marble mausoleum across the Yamuna, known as the Black Taj Mahal, originating from Jean-Baptiste Tavernier’s 1665 writings; however, excavations in the 1990s disproved the presence of blackened marble, revealing discolored white stones. In 2006, archaeologists reconstructed the Mehtab Bagh pool and confirmed a dark reflection of the white mausoleum, supporting the theory that the idea stemmed from Shah Jahan’s obsession with symmetry. There is no concrete evidence for claims that Shah Jahan mutilated or killed architects and craftsmen, nor for stories that Lord William Bentinck planned to demolish the Taj and auction its marble—such claims are linked to Bentinck’s sale of discarded Agra Fort marble. Another myth suggests that beating the finial’s silhouette will cause water to flow, with broken bangles found nearby. Several unfounded theories claim other people built the Taj Mahal, including Hindu kings like Paramardi in 1196; these were dismissed by the Supreme Court in 2000 and the Allahabad High Court in 2005. Right-wing politicians have promoted such claims, but in November 2015 and August 2017, the Union Minister of Culture and the Archaeological Survey of India respectively stated there is no evidence the monument ever housed a temple. Theories that the Taj was designed by an Italian, Geronimo Vereneo, or a Frenchman, Austin of Bordeaux, were promoted by Henry George Keene and William Henry Sleeman, based on misinterpreted texts, and later revived by Father Hosten and E. B. Havell.

The concept was first introduced by Henry George Keene in 1879, who derived it from a translation of a Spanish work, *Itinerario* (The Travels of Fray Sebastian Manrique, 1629–1643). An alternative theory, suggesting that a Frenchman named Austin of Bordeaux designed the Taj Mahal, was advanced by William Henry Sleeman, drawing upon the writings of Jean-Baptiste Tavernier. These theories were later revived by Father Hosten and further discussed by E. B. Havell, forming the foundation for subsequent debates and controversies.
